title: Tooth Pain After a Filling
meta_title: Tooth Pain After a Filling: Normal or Not? | WA Dental Care
meta_description: Cold and pressure sensitivity for days to weeks after a filling is normal. Sharp pain on biting usually means a high bite needing a quick adjustment.
intro: A tooth that is a little touchy after a filling is normal; the nerve has had a disturbance and is settling. A tooth that hurts sharply every time you bite, or aches on its own, is not settling and should be looked at. The difference between the two is easy to describe and quick to fix, so there is no reason to put up with the second kind.

sections.heading: What is usually behind it
items: **Normal settling.** Removing decay and placing a filling irritates the nerve. Cold sensitivity for a few days to a few weeks, easing steadily, is expected.
**A high bite.** The filling sits a fraction too tall, so that tooth hits first when you close. It takes the whole bite force and becomes sore. Very common and very easy to fix.
**A deep filling.** Decay that went close to the nerve leaves it inflamed; it may take longer to settle, and occasionally it does not.
**Nerve inflammation that does not reverse**, where pain lingers after cold, or throbs on its own. The tooth may need a root canal.
**A crack** in the tooth that the filling did not address, giving pain on biting and release.
**A gap or rough edge** at the margin of the filling letting cold or food in.
**Referred pain** from a neighboring tooth, or sore gum where the clamp or matrix sat.

items.title: Give normal sensitivity a little time
items.body: Mild zing from cold that fades in seconds and is a bit better each week is the nerve calming down. Avoid very cold food on that side and use a desensitizing toothpaste.

items.title: Test the bite
items.body: Tap your teeth together gently. If the filled tooth hits first, or hurts when you bite on something, that is a high filling. Call; adjusting it takes a couple of minutes and usually ends the pain the same day.

items.title: Do not wait out biting pain
items.body: A tooth left high stays sore, can become inflamed, and can crack. It is the one symptom not to be patient with.

items.title: Pain relief if needed
items.body: An over-the-counter pain reliever as labeled, if safe for you, for a tooth that aches in the first day or two.

items.title: Note the pattern
items.body: Cold only, or biting, or spontaneous? Seconds or minutes? Better or worse than last week? That tells us what is happening.

sections.heading: What happens at the visit
body: We check the bite with marking paper to see whether the filling is high, test the tooth with cold and tapping to see how the nerve is responding, look at the edges of the filling and check for a crack. A [digital X-ray](/general-dentistry/digital-x-rays/) is taken if there is any question about the nerve or the depth of the filling. Most post-filling pain is settled at this visit with a bite adjustment or a desensitizing treatment, and we tell you honestly if the nerve looks unlikely to recover.

items.title: Bite adjustment
items.body: The high spot is polished down in a couple of minutes, without numbing. The relief is usually immediate.

items.title: Desensitizing
items.body: Fluoride or desensitizing varnish on the tooth, and a desensitizing paste at home, for cold sensitivity that is slow to settle.

items.title: Watchful waiting
items.body: For a deep filling near the nerve that is improving, we recheck in a few weeks rather than intervening.

items.title: Replacing or sealing the filling
items.body: If the margin has a gap or the filling has fractured.

items.title: Root canal therapy
items.body: If the nerve is inflamed beyond recovery, root canal therapy ends the pain and keeps the tooth, usually followed by a crown on a back tooth.

items.title: A crown for a cracked tooth
items.body: If a crack is the real cause, a crown holds the tooth together.

sections.heading: Why deep fillings sometimes need more
body: When decay has reached close to the nerve, the dentist removes it and places a filling, and the nerve is given the chance to recover. Most do. A proportion, perhaps one in ten of the deepest fillings, remain inflamed and eventually need a root canal. That is not a failed filling; it is a tooth whose nerve was already too compromised, and the filling was the conservative attempt to avoid the root canal. We say this at the time of a deep filling so it is not a surprise.

faqs.q: How long should a tooth be sensitive after a filling?
faqs.a: A few days to a couple of weeks of mild cold sensitivity is typical, occasionally longer for a deep filling. It should get better week by week. Worsening pain, pain on biting or spontaneous aching are reasons to call.

faqs.q: Why does it hurt when I bite?
faqs.a: Most often the filling is slightly high and that tooth takes the whole bite. A two-minute adjustment fixes it. Less often, a crack in the tooth or inflammation of the ligament around the root is responsible, which the visit sorts out.

faqs.q: Is pain after a filling the dentist's fault?
faqs.a: Usually not. Some sensitivity is a normal response to treatment, and a slightly high bite is hard to judge when you are numb. What matters is that it is checked and corrected promptly, which is why we ask you to call rather than wait.

faqs.q: Will I need a root canal?
faqs.a: Most people do not. Root canal therapy is needed only when the nerve is inflamed beyond recovery, which shows as lingering or spontaneous pain. The tests at the visit tell us whether that is the case.

cta.heading: Sore after a filling? Call. It is usually a two-minute fix.
cta.body: Whether we placed the filling or someone else did, book a quick check and we will adjust, settle or explain what the tooth needs.
